title: Scaling a system to millions of users

facts.text: Scaling is iterative: benchmark or load test, profile for bottlenecks, address them while weighing alternatives and trade-offs, then repeat. AWS-specific details are not required, since the principles apply outside AWS too.

A user makes a read or write request; the service processes it, stores user data and returns results. It must evolve from a few users to millions, with high availability, while discussing general scaling patterns.
Assumptions: traffic is uneven and relational data is needed. The target is 10 million users, 1 billion writes and 100 billion reads per month (100:1 read to write ratio), at 1 KB per write.
The estimate is 1 TB of new content per month (1 KB per write times 1 billion writes) and 36 TB in 3 years, with 400 writes per second and 40,000 reads per second on average.
With 1-2 users, start with a single box for simplicity: a web server on EC2, storage for user data and a MySQL database, scaling vertically when needed and monitoring to find bottlenecks.

Start with SQL because relational data is needed, with MySQL on the single box. Vertical scaling (a bigger box) can get very expensive and leaves no redundancy or failover; the alternative is horizontal scaling.
An Elastic IP gives a public endpoint that survives reboots and eases failover, and DNS such as Route 53 maps the domain to it. Open only needed ports: 80, 443 and 22 for SSH from whitelisted IPs.

As users grow, vertical scaling gets expensive and blocks scaling MySQL and the web server independently. So store static content in a managed object store such as S3, and move MySQL to a separate box, for example RDS.

The split adds complexity, changes to the web server and new security needs. Secure it with encryption in transit and at rest, a Virtual Private Cloud, a public subnet for the web server and a private subnet for everything else.

When one web server bottlenecks at peak hours, scale horizontally behind a load balancer such as ELB or HAProxy, terminating SSL there. Use multiple web servers and MySQL in master-slave failover across multiple availability zones.

Separate web servers (running as reverse proxy) from application servers and scale each independently, for example read-API and write-API servers. Move static and some dynamic content to a CDN such as CloudFront.

For a read-heavy (100:1) workload, move frequently accessed content and session data to a memory cache such as ElastiCache, which makes web servers stateless, and add MySQL read replicas, splitting reads and writes in the web server.
Traffic that spikes in business hours and drops after can be handled with autoscaling groups for each web and application server type across availability zones, to keep up with spikes and cut costs.

Near the full constraints, keep a limited period of data in MySQL and the rest in a warehouse such as Redshift, and scale the memory cache for 40,000 reads per second; read replicas may struggle with cache misses.
400 writes per second may strain a single SQL write master-slave: use federation, denormalization or SQL tuning, and consider moving suitable data to NoSQL such as DynamoDB.

Work that need not be real-time goes to queues and workers: in a photo service, the application server queues a job, and a worker creates the thumbnail, updates the database and stores the thumbnail in the object store.

A simplified e-commerce site has an inventory service (product descriptions and inventory) and a user service (registration, login, user information) and evolves from a monolith on one server to a service-oriented or microservice architecture.
As the user base grows, one application server cannot handle the traffic, so the application server and the database server are moved onto two separate servers.
When one application server is still not enough, a cluster of application servers is deployed, and a load balancer routes incoming requests so each server gets an even load.
If the database becomes the bottleneck, frequent read queries are sent to read replicas by separating reads from writes, which greatly increases database write throughput.

When one database cannot carry both the inventory and user tables, the options are adding CPU and RAM (which has a hard limit), partitioning horizontally across more database servers, or adding a caching layer to offload reads.
Finally the functions are modularized into separate services, making the architecture service-oriented or microservice.

definition.text: An on-demand, configurable pool of shared resources inside a public cloud that isolates one organization's resources from the others.

facts.text: Isolation normally comes from a private IP subnet and a virtual communication construct per user, such as a VLAN or a set of encrypted channels, so the organization works as if the cloud were not shared.
A per-VPC virtual private network function secures the organization's remote access to its VPC resources through authentication and encryption.
Amazon's VPC lets EC2 instances be connected to legacy infrastructure over an IPsec VPN.
On Google Cloud a VPC is a global resource and its subnets are regional, so users connect zones and regions without extra networking complexity.
